title.title: Polynomial time algorithms for discrete logarithms and factoring on a quantum computer. (Abstract)

editorial_contributions.text:
The ``straight-line'' complexity and integer factorization of a polynomial are closely related, and polynomials are hard to evaluate if they have too many rational roots. The main result is that if, for each \(m\), there exists at least one polynomial of the form \((x- a_1) (x- a_2) \dots (x- a_m) g(x)\) with straight-line complexity less than \(\log^{O(1)} (m)\), where each \(a_i\) is a distinct rational number, then integer factorization is not sufficiently hard for cryptographic purposes. 


Let \(f(x_1, \dots, x_n)\) be a polynomial over \(\mathbb{Q}\). A straight-line computation of length \(m\) for the polynomial \(f(x_1, \dots, x_n)\) is a sequence of rational functions \(g_1, \dots, g_m\) such that \(f= g_m\) and either (i) \(g_i=1\) or \(g_i= x_j\) or (ii) \(g_i= g_j * g_k\) where \(j,k< i\) and \(*\in \{+, -, \times\}\). The straight-line complexity \(L(f)\) of \(f(x_1, \dots, x_n)\) is the length of the shortest such computation. If \(x= a/b\) is a rational number then \(\text{height} (x)\) is defined to be \(|a|+ |b|\). 


The main result consists of the following theorem. A sequence of monic polynomials \(\{f_m (x)\}\) is a \(c\)-sequence provided \(\deg (f_m (x))\leq 2^{\log^c (m)}\) and there are distinct rational roots \(a_1, \dots, a_m\) of \(f_m (x)\) such that, for all \(i\), \(j\), \(\text{height} (a_i- a_j)\leq 2^{\log^c (m)}\). 


Theorem 1 (Root Theorem). Suppose that factoring is hard. Let \(\{f_m (x)\}\) be a \(c\)-sequence of polynomials. Then, for any constant \(d>0\), 
\[
L(f_m (x))\geq \log^d (m),
\]
 for \(m\) large enough. (This means that a polynomial with many rational roots cannot be easy to evaluate.) 


The Root Theorem is proved and two applications are given. (1) Many interesting polynomials are hard to evaluate; for example, it follows from the Root Theorem that for any \(c>0\) the polynomial \((x-1) (x-2) \dots (x-n)\) requires \(\Omega (\log^c (n))\) steps to compute. (2) Let \(P(G; x)\) denote the chromatic polynomial that counts the number of possible ways to colour the graph \(G\) with \(x\) colours, let \(G_n\) be a sequence of \(n\)-vertex graphs and suppose \(G_n\) requires at least \(2^{\log^\varepsilon (n)}\) colours for some \(\varepsilon> 0\). Then it follows from the Root Theorem that for any \(d>0\), \(L(P( G_n; x))\geq \Omega (\log^d (n))\).

title.title: Computing in the Jacobian of a plane algebraic curve. (Extended abstract)

editorial_contributions.text:
The author is very at ease with using \(2 \times 2\) matrices to deal with continued fractions. He wrote a few papers dealing with that idea, showing each time how efficient and useful it is, how faster it could be; he could even state some results otherwise hardly predictable without this approach. Once again, the wizard shows his magic: he exhibits infinite families of integers \(M\) (function of many integers) for which he can predict the fundamental unit of the real quadratic field \(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt M)\), thereby generalizing many results of about ten previous authors. The experts with continued fractions will certainly enjoy this nicely written paper.

title.title: Explicit formulas for units in certain quadratic number fields

editorial_contributions.text:
Let \(K\) be a field, let \(f \in K[x]\) be a polynomial of odd degree \(n = 2g + 1\) without multiple roots, let \(H\) be the smooth projective curve associated with \(y^2 - f\), then \(H\) is a hyperelliptic curve of genus \(g\). Let \(K(H)\) be the function field of \(H\) over \(K\), let \(J = J_K (H)\) be the divisors of degree 0 modulo the principal divisors of \(K(H)\), then \(J\) is isomorphic as a group to the group of rational points on the Jacobian of \(H\). If \(g = 1\) then \(H\) is an elliptic curve. It will be assumed that \(K\) is a finite field and hence that \(J = J_K (H)\) is a finite group.


Given two elements \(\alpha, \beta\) in \(J\) the discrete logarithm problem is to calculate an \(r \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\) (if such exists) such that \(r \alpha = \beta\). An algorithm is presented that is subexponential for curves of high genus and for the case that \(K\) is a prime field of characteristic not equal to two (although generalization to arbitrary finite fields seems straightforward). An heuristic argument is given that under certain assumptions, there exists a \(c \in \mathbb{R}_{> 0}\) such that for all sufficiently large \(g \in \mathbb{Z}_{> 0}\), for all odd primes \(p\) with \(\log p \leq (2g + 1)^{.98}\), the algorithm computes discrete logarithms in the group of rational points on the Jacobian of a genus \(g\) hyperelliptic curve over \(GF (p)\) with expected time \(L_{p^{2g + 1}} [1/2, c]\) where \(c \leq 2.181\).

editorial_contributions.text:
The modular interpolation approach to multivariate polynomial factorization uses interpolation to combine many univariate factorizations. The classical Hilbert irreducibility theorem guarantees that in most cases the univariate factorizations have the same structure as the multivariate factorization. The new algorithm is more straightforward than previous algorithms and has comparable computational complexity. 


Suppose we seek the factorization of \(P\in L[X, Y_1, \dots,Y_n]\) over the field \(L\). Let \((y_1, \dots, y_n)\in L^n\) be a random \(n\)-tuple. The first step is to produce a black box 
\[
{\mathcal B}: (y_1, \dots, y_n) \mapsto \{\text{factors }P_i,\;i=1, \dots, k, \text{ of } P(X, y_1, \dots, y_n )\}.
\]
 For different inputs, the \(P_i\) may be returned in different orders. The techniques of \textit{S. Ar}, \textit{R. J. Lipton} and \textit{M. Sudan} [Reconstructing algebraic functions from mixed data, 33rd ACM Symp. Found. Comput. Sci. 503-512 (1992)]\ are used to construct \(k\) black boxes that each represent an individual factor \(P_i\) of \(P\). The black boxes can then be interpolated using sparse polynomial interpolation. 


Let \(L= \mathbb{Q}\). If the factorization of \(P(X, y_1, \dots, y_n)\) has no more factors than that of 


\(P(X, Y_1, \dots,Y_n)\) then call \((y_1, \dots, y_n)\) Hilbertian for \(P\). Let the number of non-Hilbertian \(n\)-tuples with \(0\leq y_i< N\) for an irreducible polynomial of degree \(d\) be \(\overline {R} (d, n, N)\). Then the number of such \(n\)-tuples for a general polynomial \(P\) with \(k\) irreducible factors is \(R(d, n, N)\leq k\overline {R} (d, n,N)\). 


Proposition 1. Let \(P\in \mathbb{Q}[X, Y_1, \dots, Y_n ]\) and the degree of \(X\) in \(P\) be less than \(d\). Let \(a_1, \dots, a_n\in \mathbb{Z}\). For sufficiently large \(N\), the number of \(n\)-tuples \((y_1, \dots, y_n)\in \mathbb{Z}^n\), \(a_i\leq y_i< N+ a_i\), for which \(P(X, y_1, \dots, y_n)\) factors differently from \(P(X, Y_1, \dots,Y_n)\) is less than 
\[
R(d, n, N)< c(d, n) N^{n- {1\over 2}}\log N.
\]
 This follows from a result by \textit{S. D. Cohen} [Proc. Lond. Math. Soc., III. Ser. 43, 227-250 (1981; Zbl 0484.12002)]. Hence the values used in the interpolation must be chosen randomly from a large enough domain. If the conjecture that \(c(d, n)< c_1 d^{c_2} n^{c_3}\) is true then the algorithm presented runs in random polynomial time. 


Assume for simplicity of exposition that \(P\) is monic and squarefree. (The extension to non-monic polynomials is outlined in an appendix.) For any Hilbertian \({\mathbf y}= (y_1, \dots, y_n)\) let \(P(X, {\mathbf y})= P_{1{\mathbf y}} (X) P_{2{\mathbf y}} (X) \cdots P_{k{\mathbf y}} (X)\). Construct a polynomial multivalued black box \({\mathcal B}\) to return the unordered set of factors \({\mathcal B} ({\mathbf y})= \{P_{1{\mathbf y}} (X), P_{2{\mathbf y}} (X), \dots, P_{k{\mathbf y}} (X)\}\). The problem of recovering the multivariate factors by interpolation is approached bottom-up. 


The first problem is this: given a collection of \(t\) unordered \(k\)-tuples of values \(\{q_i (\theta)\}\), \(\theta\in \mathbb{Z}\), returned by a black box \({\mathcal B}\), determine the corresponding \(k\)-tuples of univariate polynomials \(\{q_i (\Theta)\}\). Brute force requires time exponential in \(t\) because the \(k\)-tuples are unordered. However, from \(\{q_i (\theta)\}\) the values of all the symmetric functions \(\{\sigma_i (\theta)\}\) of the \(\{q_i (\theta)\}\) can be computed without regard to their order and the symmetric function values can then be interpolated to symmetric polynomials \(\{\sigma_i (\Theta)\}\). From these polynomials, the bivariate polynomial 
\[
\begin{aligned} Q(Z, \Theta) &= Z^k- \sigma_1 (\Theta) Z^{k-1}+ \cdots+ (-1)^k \sigma_k (\Theta)\\ &= (Z- q_1 (\Theta)) \cdots (Z- q_k (\Theta)) \end{aligned}
\]
 can be constructed. The known zeros \(\{q_i (\theta)\}\) of \(Q(Z, \theta)\) can be refined to zeros of \(Q (Z, \Theta)\) using Newton's iteration (essentially Hensel lifting), the details of which are given in the appendix. 


Multivalued black boxes of multivariate polynomials are interpolated by ordering their output, as follows. The point \({\mathbf y}= (y_1, \dots, y_m)\) is called a reference point if, for all \(i\), \(j\), \(p_i({\mathbf y}) \neq p_j({\mathbf y)}\). Reference points can be found by random choice and verification. For each black box \({\mathcal M}\) compute the ordered sequence of reference values \({\mathcal M} ({\mathbf y})= \langle p_1 ({\mathbf y}), \dots, p_k ({\mathbf y}) \rangle\). Apply univariate black box interpolation to \({\mathcal M} ({\mathbf y}+ \theta ({\mathbf x}- {\mathbf y}))\) to determine the unordered set of univariate polynomials 
\[
S_{\mathbf x}= \{p_1 ({\mathbf y}+ \Theta ({\mathbf x}- {\mathbf y})), \dots, p_k ({\mathbf y}+ \Theta ({\mathbf x}- {\mathbf y} ))\}.
\]
 Substitute \(\Theta=0\) and compare with the reference values of order \(S_{\mathbf x}\) and then substitute \(\Theta=1\) to determine the ordered set of values \(p_1 ({\mathbf x}), \dots, p_k ({\mathbf x})\). Conventional interpolation can then be used to recover the polynomials. 


Finally, the case of polynomial multivalued black boxes is best handled as follows. If \(d\) is the maximum degree of \(X\) in any \(P_i (X, Y_1, \dots, Y_n)\) then replace the polynomial-valued black box by \(d+1\) \(\mathbb{Q}\)-multivalued black boxes corresponding to their coefficients with respect to \(X\). The polynomials (in \(Y_1, \dots, Y_n)\) represented by these black boxes can be reconstructed using the previous techniques. 


Proposition 2. Let \(P(X_1, \dots, X_n)\) be a multivariate polynomial over \(\mathbb{Q}\), where the total degree of \(P\) is bounded by \(D\), the sum of the absolute values of the coefficients in \(P\) is bounded by \(H\), and the maximum number of non-zero terms in any factor is \(T\). Then \(P\) can be factored into irreducible components in \(O(n^3 (D^{8+ \varepsilon} HT+ nD^3 T^3)\) arithmetic operations (for any \(\varepsilon> 0)\). With classical integer multiplication \(O(n^3 D^{9+ \varepsilon} HT+ nD^3 T^3)\) arithmetic operations are required.

title.title: Decomposition of algebraic functions

editorial_contributions.text:
A ``witness'', \(a\) say, for an odd composite number \(n\), is an integer, not a multiple of \(n\), for which \(n\) is not a strong pseudoprime to base \(a\). The first result of the paper is that, for any \(K\), there are infinitely many Carmichael numbers for which the first witness exceeds \(K\). Indeed a more quantitative form of this statement is proved. Assuming a certain uniform version of the prime triplets conjecture it is shown that there are positive constants \(a\) and \(b\) so that there are at least \(x^a\) Carmichael numbers \(n \leq x\) for which the smallest witness exceeds \(b \log x\). Finally, answering a question of Lenstra, it is shown that, for \(x > x(K)\), there can be no set of \(K\) integers which includes witnesses for all the odd composite integers up to \(x\). Again, a more quantitative form of this assertion is given. The proofs depend on the authors' construction [Ann. Math. (2) 139, No. 3, 703-722 (1994; Zbl 0816.11005)] of infinitely many Carmichael numbers.

editorial_contributions.text:
Let \(z_0\) be chosen randomly in the disc \(|z|\leq 1\) (with \(\text{Im} (z)\neq 0\)) and let \(U\) be the transformation \(U(z)= z^{-1}- [\text{Re} (z)^{-1} ]\). \(z_1= U(z_0)\), \(z_0= U(z_1), \dots\) are computed until \(|z_k |>1\). This corresponds to reducing a random lattice in two dimensions to one with minimal basis. Let \(\mu\) denote the expected number of iterations required, and let \(\omega_k\) denote the probability that \((k+1)\) or more iterations will be required. The \(\omega_i\) are calculated in terms of the continuants of continued fractions; an operator previously studied by \textit{D. H. Mayer} [in Ergodic theory, symbolic dynamics, and hyperbolic spaces, Lect. Workshop Hyperbolic Geom. Ergodic Theory, Trieste/Italy 1989, 175-222 (1991; Zbl 0755.58034)]\ is also used and the \(\omega_i\) are expressed in terms of its eigenvalues. The authors have evaluated \(\mu\) to 50 decimal places, and \(\omega_1\), \(\omega_2\), \(\omega_3\) to 20 decimal places. \(10^8\) simulations gave results in very close agreement with the theoretical values. The authors also consider a centred algorithm in which the transformation \(U(z)= U(z) (\text{sgn(Re} (z^{-1})- \{\text{Re} (z^{-1})\})\) is used where \(\{\;\}\) denotes the nearest integer. 


No proofs are given.

The author presents an algorithm for computing discrete logarithms over finite fields of the form \(GF (p^n)\) called the function field sieve. This new algorithm is related to the number field sieve methods used in integer factorization [cf. \textit{A. K. Lenstra} and \textit{H. W. Lenstra jun.} (eds.), The development of the number field sieve, Lect. Notes Math. 1554, Springer (1993; Zbl 0777.00017 and Zbl 0806.11067)]. The function field sieve method for discrete logarithms has a heuristic expected running time of \(\exp [O((n \log p)^{1/3} (\log (n \log p))^{2/3})]\), with the requirement that \(\log p \leq n^{g(n)}\) where \(g\) is a positive, real-valued function that is bounded above by 0.98 and approaches zero as \(n \to \infty\).

title.title: Counting the number of points on elliptic curves over finite fields of characteristic greater than three

editorial_contributions.text:
Let \(E\) be an elliptic curve over a finite field \(\mathbb{F}_p\) where \(p\) is a large prime number. Schoof's algorithm computes the number \(N\) of \(\mathbb{F}_p\)-rational points on \(E\) by calculating \(N\) modulo \(l\) for sufficiently many small prime numbers \(l\). The calculation of \(N\) modulo \(l\) uses the connection of \(N\) with the Frobenius endomorphism \(\pi_E\) acting on the \(l\)-adic Tate module of \(E\). The improvement of Atkin and Elkies makes use of those prime numbers \(l\) (called ``good primes''), where the eigenvalues of \(\pi_E\) are contained in \(\mathbb{Z}_l\). In this paper the authors propose a strategy which in addition makes use of higher powers \(l^n\) of ``good primes'' \(l\).

title.title: Schoof's algorithm and isogeny cycles

editorial_contributions.text:
The sieve of Eratosthenes is often used to identify the primes up to a given limit \(N\). It is an additive algorithm in the sense that it requires some \(\Theta(N\log\log N)\) additions of numbers of size \(O(N)\), but multiplications are not used. The author [Commun. ACM 24, 18--23 (1981; Zbl 0454.68084); Acta Inf. 17, 477--485 (1982; Zbl 0489.10007)]\ gave his `wheel sieve' which is sublinear, i.e., \(o(N)\), and additive. \textit{S. Bengelloun} [Acta Inf. 23, 119--125 (1986; Zbl 0601.10004)]\ then promoted the notion of being incremental, meaning that \(N\) need not be fixed, so that the algorithm can be run indefinitely to enumerate the primes. Actually any sieve algorithm can be made incremental by repeatedly running it with a doubled limit, but Bengelloun gave a `smoothly' incremental one in the sense that it takes bounded time to progress from \(N\) to \(N+1\). His smoothly incremental sieve requires \(\Theta (N)\) multiplications and additions. 


Here the author gives an algorithm which is \(\Theta (N/ \log\log N)\), additive and smoothly incremental. Bengelloun's linear algorithm is modified by the elimination of multiplications with the introduction of calculated differences using a multiplication table, the incremental growth of which is not too rapid according to theorems on prime gaps. Reduced residue systems of products of the primes up to a limit that grows with \(N\) are then used to reduce the complexity to being sublinear while still being smoothly incremental.

title.title: Constructing elliptic curves with given group order over large finite fields

editorial_contributions.text:
This paper addresses the question of how to reduce the basis of a non- integral lattice. The idea is to first compute a rational approximation of the basis matrix of the lattice, and then use one of the standard lattice-basis reduction algorithms such as Korkine-Zolotarev or LLL on the approximation. The resulting reduced basis is not useful, but the reducing unimodular transformation that is constructed in the process can be applied to the original, non-integral basis of the lattice. The question, then, is whether this transformation will reduce the non- integral basis as it does the approximation. 


Let \(A\) be a rational approximation to a basis \(B\) of a \(k\)-dimensional lattice in \(\mathbb{R}^m\). Assume \(A\) has rank \(k\), and a lattice-basis reduction algorithm applied to the columns of \(A\) yields a transformation \(T= (\text{t}_1, \dots, \text{t}_k)\in GL(k, \mathbb{Z})\). Further, \(T\) and \(A\) satisfy the inequality \(A\text{t}_i\leq s_i \lambda_i (L (A))\) for \(1\leq i\leq k\), where \(L(A)\) is the lattice generated by the columns of \(A\), \(s_i\geq 1\), and \(\lambda_i (L (A))\) is the \(i\)-th successive minimum of that lattice. Let \(c>0\). This paper presents results on how closely \(A\) must approximate \(B\) in order to guarantee that \(B\text{t}_i\leq (1+ c) s_i \lambda_i (L(B))\).

title.title: Computing the degree of a modular parametrization

editorial_contributions.text:
Let \(K\) be an algebraic number field of degree \(n\) over the field of rational numbers \(\mathbb{Q}\), and let \(Z_K\) be its ring of integers. For an integer ideal \({\mathfrak q}\), denote by \(\Lambda_{\mathfrak q}\) the residue ring modulo \({\mathfrak q}\) and by \(\Lambda^*_{\mathfrak q}\) the multiplicative group of units of this ring. It is known that \(|\Lambda_{\mathfrak q}|= Nm ({\mathfrak q})\) and \(|\Lambda^*_{\mathfrak q}|= \varphi ({\mathfrak q})\) where \(\varphi (\cdot)\) is the Euler function in \(Z_K\). Given a finitely generated semigroup \(V\) of \(Z_K\) 
\[
V= \{\lambda_1^{x_1} \cdots \lambda_r^{x_r} \mid x_1, \dots, x_r\geq 0\}.
\]
 Denote its reduction modulo \({\mathfrak q}\) by \(V_{\mathfrak q}\). Assume the generators are linearly independent. Various bounds on character sums are used to obtain results on the distribution of the residues of elements of \(V\) modulo an integer ideal \({\mathfrak q}\). When \(K= \mathbb{Q}\) and \(r=1\) this is the distribution of the residues of an exponential function. Besides this, several other problems from algebraic number theory, the theory of function fields over a finite field, complexity theory, cryptography and coding theory where results on the distribution of some group \(V\) modulo \({\mathfrak q}\) play a central role are considered.

title.title: Efficient checking of computations in number theory. (Abstract)

editorial_contributions.text:
The following algorithm for computing the greatest common divisor of two integers is proposed and analyzed. Given \(u,v \in \mathbb{N}\), \(u \geq v > 0\), let \(e \in \mathbb{N}\) be the unique exponent such that \(2^{e - 1} v \leq u < 2^ev\); now put \(u = \max \{v,t\}\), \(v = \min \{v,t\}\) where \(t\) is the smaller one of the remainders \(u - 2^{e - 1}v\), \(2^e v - u\), and iterate this procedure until \(v = 0\). Th final value of \(u\) obtained in this way is the g.c.d. of the given pair. For binary representations of \(u\) and \(v\) the algorithm clearly requires only (left) shifts and subtractions.


Define \((u_n, v_n)\), \(u_n \geq v_n > 0\), to be the lexicographically least pair that requires the algorithm to perform \(n\) steps. The authors determine these worst-case inputs explicitly in terms of their continued fraction expansions. The proof makes use of a result concerning the extremality of certain continuants [the reviewer, Proc. Am. Math. Soc. 89, 189-201 (1983; Zbl 0514.10002)] which is adapted in a clever way to the present situation.

title.title: Analysis of a left-shift binary GCD algorithm

editorial_contributions.text:
The computational problem of factoring a one-variable polynomial \(f\) over the finite field \(k\) into irreducible factors over \(k\) is considered. A finite field of cardinality \(q = p^m\) is explicitly given if, for some basis of \(k\) over its prime subfield, the product of two basis elements in the basis is given. So far as is known, the only general deterministic algorithms for factoring an arbitrary polynomial of degree \(n\) over an explicitly given finite field of cardinality \(p^m\) are those of Berlekamp and Rónyai. While the former is polynomial for small \(p\) and the latter is polynomial for small \(n\), both are exponential if no restrictions are made.


The following theorem is shown: Theorem: Assuming GRH there exists a deterministic algorithm which, given a polynomial \(f\) of degree \(n\) over an explicitly given finite field \(k\) of cardinality \(q\), decomposes \(f\) into irreducible factors over \(k\) in time \((n^{\log n} \log q)^{O (1)}\).


Since the GRH is needed only to take roots in a finite field, the result can be formulated that a polynomial equation over a finite field can be solved by radicals in subexponential time.

title.title: Factorization of polynomials over finite fields in subexponential time under GRH

editorial_contributions.text:
It was shown by \textit{J. A. Buchmann} and \textit{H. C. Williams} [J. Complexity 7, 311-315 (1991; Zbl 0744.11067)]\ that certain problems connected with ideals and class groups in quadratic fields belonged, assuming a generalized Riemann hypothesis, to the complexity class \(\text{NP}\cap \text{coNP}\). In the present paper this is extended, so far as the verification of class number is concerned, to fields of any degree. 


In order to do this the author gives a compact representation of algebraic integers so as to bound the number of bits necessary to represent a system of fundamental units. This is done by using the theory of minima in ideals described by \textit{J. A. Buchmann} in his Habilitationsschrift, Düsseldorf (1987).
